and-but-or.title: Conjunctions: AND, BUT & OR
and-but-or.description: Build clear connections between ideas using addition, contrast and alternatives.
questions: The online guide includes maps ___ short safety videos.
Use and to add a second, related item to the list.
I wanted to walk home, ___ it started pouring with rain.
Use but to connect two ideas that contrast: you wanted to walk, but the weather changed.
You can submit your reflection as a video ___ a short essay.
The library was quiet, ___ we finished the group report there.
Use and to connect two related facts. The comma is not required here because the second clause is closely linked and the sentence is short.
The new app is easy to use, ___ some features are hard to find.
Use but to show a contrast between the app's ease of use and the difficulty of finding some features.
Would you rather work alone ___ with a partner?
Use or to offer two possible choices.
Daniel checked the instructions ___ opened the file.
Use and to add a second action performed by the same person.
She practised every day, ___ she still felt nervous before the presentation.
Use but to contrast her preparation with her continued nervousness.
Take an umbrella ___ a raincoat with you.
Use or when either of two alternatives is possible.
The club welcomes beginners ___ experienced players.
Use and to include both groups.
I understand your point, ___ I see the problem differently.
Use but to introduce a different viewpoint.
Is the meeting in the library ___ in the computer lab?
Use or to ask the listener to choose between two locations.
We designed the poster ___ recorded a short announcement.
Use and to connect two actions in the same sequence.
The instructions look simple, ___ read them carefully before you begin.
Use but to introduce a warning that contrasts with the apparent simplicity.
You can ask Ms. Rivera ___ send your question by email.
Use or to present two ways of asking for help.
Use and to combine two positive descriptions.
The route is shorter, ___ it is less safe at night.
Use but to show that the shorter route has a disadvantage.
We can begin now ___ wait until the rest of the team arrives.
Use or to present two possible actions.
The team collected the data ___ organized it in a chart.
Use and to join two actions carried out by the team.
The instructions were clear, ___ several students misunderstood the final step.
Use but to contrast the clarity of the instructions with the unexpected result.
Do you want to print the report ___ upload it?
Use or to offer two ways to submit the report.
The school provides tablets, ___ students can also borrow laptops.
Use and to add another available resource.
I had prepared my notes, ___ I forgot to bring them.
Use but to show the contrast between preparing the notes and forgetting them.
The coach shared the schedule ___ explained how to register.
And connects two related actions: sharing the schedule and explaining registration.
Both the science club ___ the music club will perform at the school fair.
And joins the two parts of a compound subject.
The new library has study rooms ___ a quiet area for group projects.
And adds another feature to the list.
The hotel was fully booked, ___ the receptionist found us another place nearby.
But introduces an unexpected contrast between the lack of rooms and the helpful solution.
The device is lightweight, ___ it is powerful enough for video editing.
Would you prefer to present first ___ speak after the break?
Students may work with the printed article ___ use the online version.
Or connects two ways of working.

because.title: Conjunctions: BECAUSE
because.description: Explain reasons clearly and connect causes to the ideas they support.
questions: The match was postponed ___ the field was too wet to use.
Because introduces the reason the match was postponed.
Nina reviewed her notes twice ___ she wanted to feel prepared.
Because explains Nina's reason for reviewing her notes.
We left the room quietly ___ another class was taking an exam.
Because introduces the reason for leaving quietly.
Carlos took a jacket ___ the evening forecast predicted cooler weather.
Because gives the reason Carlos took a jacket.
The students used the library ___ they needed reliable sources for the project.
Because introduces the reason the students chose the library.
I saved the document twice ___ I did not want to lose my work.
Because explains why the document was saved twice.
The bus was crowded ___ many people were travelling to the festival.
Because introduces the cause of the crowded bus.
Maya chose the science elective ___ she enjoys doing experiments.
Because tells us why Maya chose the elective.
The team practised indoors ___ heavy rain had made the court slippery.
Because gives the reason for practising indoors.
We arrived early ___ we wanted to find seats together.
Because explains the group's reason for arriving early.
The website was difficult to navigate ___ several links were not working.
Because introduces the cause of the navigation problem.
Leo wore comfortable shoes ___ the tour involved a long walk.
Because gives the reason Leo chose comfortable shoes.
The teacher repeated the instructions ___ some students had not heard them clearly.
Because explains why the teacher repeated the instructions.
The café was nearly empty ___ most customers were watching the match at home.
Because introduces the reason the café was quiet.
I turned off my notifications ___ I needed to concentrate on the assignment.
Because explains why the notifications were turned off.
The team selected a different location ___ the original room was too small.
Because provides the reason for changing the location.
We carried reusable bottles ___ the event encouraged visitors to reduce plastic waste.
Because explains why the visitors brought reusable bottles.
Sofia asked for feedback ___ she wanted to improve her final draft.
Because introduces Sofia's purpose or reason for asking.
The presentation started late ___ the projector needed to be restarted.
Because gives the reason the presentation started late.
I checked the timetable again ___ the departure platform had changed.
Because introduces the reason for checking the timetable again.
The players rested for a few minutes ___ the first half had been exhausting.
Because explains why the players rested.
The store extended its opening hours ___ many customers requested more time to shop.
Because provides the reason the store changed its hours.
We chose the train ___ it was more comfortable for a long journey.
Because explains the reason for choosing the train.
The volunteers wore name tags ___ visitors could identify them easily.
Because introduces the reason for wearing name tags.
I brought a printed copy ___ the internet connection was unreliable.
Because gives the reason for bringing a printed copy.
The students celebrated ___ their team had won the regional competition.
Because introduces the reason for celebrating.
The guide spoke slowly ___ several visitors were learning English.
Because explains why the guide spoke slowly.
We moved the meeting online ___ a number of participants were working remotely.
Because gives the reason for moving the meeting online.
The road was closed ___ construction workers were repairing the bridge.
Because introduces the cause of the road closure.
Amir chose the earlier appointment ___ he had another commitment that afternoon.
Because explains why Amir chose the earlier appointment.

fanboys-foundations.title: FANBOYS: All Seven Coordinating Conjunctions
fanboys-foundations.description: Practise for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so through clear, everyday situations.
questions: The team moved the equipment indoors, ___ the forecast warned of a storm.
For is a coordinating conjunction that introduces a reason. It is more formal than because.
The presentation included a short video ___ a live demonstration.
And adds a second, related element to the presentation.
The report did not include a budget, ___ did it list the project deadlines.
Nor adds a second negative idea. Notice the auxiliary inversion: nor did it list.
The instructions were brief, ___ they covered every important step.
But introduces a contrast between the short instructions and how much they covered.
You can save the document online ___ download a copy to your device.
The trail was steep, ___ the younger students reached the summit.
Yet highlights an unexpected contrast: the trail was steep, but the students succeeded.
The school Wi-Fi stopped working, ___ the class used mobile data.
So introduces the result of the Wi-Fi problem.
Marta revised the introduction ___ checked the final paragraph.
And links two actions performed by the same person.
The café looked crowded, ___ we found an empty table near the window.
But shows that the result was different from what the crowded café suggested.
Should we meet before class, ___ would lunchtime be better?
Or introduces the second option in a question.
I saved a second copy, ___ the first file had become corrupted.
For gives the reason for saving another copy.
He cannot attend the workshop, ___ can he join the online session.
Nor follows a negative statement and introduces another negative possibility. Use inversion: nor can he.
The instructions were unclear, ___ the teacher demonstrated the process.
So connects a situation with the action taken as a result.
The phone is several years old, ___ its battery still lasts all day.
Yet emphasizes the surprising contrast between the phone's age and its battery life.
The volunteers collected old books ___ delivered them to the community center.
The new rule is stricter, ___ it is easier for everyone to understand.
You must confirm your place today, ___ the system may release your reservation.
Or presents the consequence of not taking the first action: confirm today or risk losing the place.
The group chose a quieter room, ___ the recording needed clear audio.
For introduces the reason behind the group's choice.
The article did not mention the deadline, ___ did it explain how to apply.
Nor adds another negative statement. The auxiliary did comes before the subject.
The bus was delayed by traffic, ___ we arrived ten minutes late.
So introduces the result of the traffic delay.
The task looked difficult, ___ most students completed it without help.
Yet highlights the unexpected success despite the apparent difficulty.
The science club meets on Tuesdays ___ organizes a project fair each term.
And adds another fact about the science club.
I checked the address twice, ___ I still went to the wrong building.
But connects the careful checking with an unexpected mistake.
We can use the school printer, ___ we can send the file to the copy shop.
Or links two possible ways to print the file.
Please keep your voice low, ___ another class is taking a test nearby.
For gives the reason for speaking quietly.
The device was not charged, ___ was the spare battery available.
Nor adds a second negative situation and uses inversion: nor was the spare battery.
The deadline was moved forward, ___ everyone had to reorganize their schedule.
So introduces the result of the earlier deadline.
The instructions were detailed, ___ a few important questions remained unanswered.
Yet shows an unexpected contrast between the detailed instructions and the remaining questions.
The students interviewed local residents ___ summarized their findings.
And joins two actions in the students' project.
The first solution was inexpensive, ___ it did not solve the main problem.
But introduces the disadvantage of the inexpensive solution.

fanboys-clauses.title: FANBOYS: Joining Clauses & Punctuation
fanboys-clauses.description: Choose the right connector and notice when a comma is needed between independent clauses.
questions: The student reviewed the rubric ___ corrected the citations.
One subject performs both actions, so and joins the verbs. Do not place a comma between these two verbs.
The deadline was close, ___ the team submitted the draft that afternoon.
Both sides can stand as complete sentences. Use a comma before so when it joins these independent clauses and shows a result.
Please bring a pencil ___ a calculator to the workshop.
Or joins two noun phrases, not two independent clauses. No comma is needed.
The student did not complain, ___ did she ask for a refund.
Nor links a second negative independent clause. Use a comma before nor and invert the auxiliary: nor did she ask.
The room was small, ___ it accommodated the entire group.
But joins two complete clauses that contrast. Place a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
Liam ___ his cousin volunteered to organize the event.
And joins two parts of a compound subject. No comma is needed between the subject nouns.
The trip was cancelled, ___ the road had become unsafe after the storm.
For joins two independent clauses and gives a reason. Place a comma before for.
The instructions were detailed, ___ several students still needed help.
Yet introduces a surprising contrast between two complete clauses. Use a comma before yet.
The server stopped responding, ___ the technician restarted it.
So joins two complete clauses and introduces the result. Use a comma before so.
We can present the results today, ___ we can wait until Monday.
Or joins two independent alternatives. The comma before or separates the complete clauses.
The editor checked the facts ___ corrected two spelling errors.
A single subject performs both actions. And joins the verbs, so no comma is needed.
The first draft was clear, ___ it did not include any supporting evidence.
Both sides are complete clauses with contrasting information. Use a comma before but.
The team had not tested the link, ___ had it checked the form on a phone.
Nor introduces another negative clause. Use a comma before it and invert the auxiliary: nor had it checked.
I closed the windows, ___ the wind was blowing rain into the classroom.
For introduces an explanation as a second independent clause. A comma comes before for.
The candidate had little experience, ___ she answered every question confidently.
Yet marks an unexpected contrast between two complete clauses. Place a comma before it.
You may email the form ___ leave a printed copy at reception.
Or connects two verb phrases with the same subject. No comma is needed.
The projector would not connect, ___ the teacher shared the slides on screen.
So links the problem and its result. Since both sides are independent clauses, use a comma before so.
The first group finished early, ___ the second group requested more time.
And joins two related independent clauses. Use a comma before and.
Nora opened the document ___ highlighted the sections that needed revision.
The same subject performs both actions. Use and for addition, and do not add a comma between the verbs.
The notice did not explain the new procedure, ___ did it provide a contact number.
Nor adds a second negative independent clause. The auxiliary did comes before the subject.
We moved the meeting online, ___ several participants were travelling.
For introduces the reason for the decision. A comma separates the independent clauses.
The instructions were short, ___ they covered every required safety measure.
Yet emphasizes the unexpected contrast. The two independent clauses are separated by a comma.
You can revise the opening paragraph, ___ you can rewrite the conclusion first.
Or joins two complete alternative actions. Use a comma before or.
The class brainstormed ideas, selected a topic ___ planned the presentation.
And completes a series of actions. The conjunction joins the final two items in the series.
The website looked professional, ___ its contact information was out of date.
But links two complete clauses that contrast. Use a comma before but.
The instructions were confusing, ___ the teacher gave a second example.
So introduces the result of the confusing instructions. Use a comma before so.
The hallway was unusually quiet, ___ the final exam had already begun.
For gives the explanation in a second independent clause. Use a comma before for.
She had never used the software, ___ had she received any training.
Nor adds a second negative idea. The auxiliary had is inverted before the subject.
The team had limited resources, ___ it completed the project ahead of schedule.
Yet introduces an unexpected contrast between limited resources and early completion.
Would you prefer a written summary ___ a short audio explanation?
Or connects two noun phrases as alternatives. No comma is needed between them.
